Chapter 9: Class, Race, and the Politics of Division
Let’s dig into a story that’s about a lot more than just class. When you hear the term “white trash,” it’s tempting to think it’s only about poverty or status. But really, it’s woven through with questions of race—and the ways class and race have always worked together to shape American life.
Imagine a small community where neighbors take care of each other, sharing what little they’ve got. Now, picture outside forces—politicians, employers, even the media—coming in and stirring things up. They spread a message that feels all too familiar: there’s not enough for everyone, so you’d better fight for your slice.
When you look back through American history, you’ll notice a pattern. The powerful—those at the top—have used class and race like tools, keeping working people divided. Poor whites were told their skin color gave them a special place, even though they were still shut out of real opportunities. At the same time, they were warned that if Black folks or immigrants gained anything, it would come straight out of their pockets.
And here’s the thing: this approach has worked, time and time again. By getting everyday people to focus on what separates them, those in power hold on to their own spot at the top. Most folks never see how these divisions are made, or how they’re used to benefit a select few.
Fast forward to today, and you’ll see those old tactics are alive and well. Just listen to the debates about immigration, policing, or voting rights. These aren’t just policy issues—they’re often framed to set one group against another. Words like “real Americans” or “outsiders” get thrown around to make some people feel like they belong, and push others out.
But it’s not all division. Every so often, there are sparks of solidarity—moments when people look past the lines of race and class and come together to demand something better. These moments might not last long, but they remind us of what’s possible if we can break down those old barriers.
The story of “white trash” is really a lesson: those lines between class and race? They aren’t set in stone. They’re put there—and kept there—by people who benefit from keeping us apart. Breaking down those walls isn’t easy, but it is possible. And every step we take toward that is a step toward real change.
